title: When Does Conformer Geometry Help? Complementarity of 3D Ensemble Statistics and 2D Fingerprints for Molecular Property Prediction

paper.title: When Does Conformer Geometry Help? Complementarity of 3D Ensemble Statistics and 2D Fingerprints for Molecular Property Prediction
paper.abstract:
Abstract. When do three-dimensional conformer ensembles improve molecular property prediction beyond two-dimensional fingerprints?
We provide the first systematic, mechanistically grounded answer.
Through ∼ {\sim} 1,000 experiments spanning 13 model configurations, 14 regression targets, and 2 classification targets across MoleculeNet, QM9, and MARCEL benchmarks, we discover selective complementarity : conformer ensemble statistics extracted via Distribution Kernel Operators (DKOs) yield statistically significant RMSE reductions on solvation-dependent properties (ESOL − 11.0 % -11.0\% , p < 10 − 9 p<10^{-9} ; FreeSolv − 13.5 % -13.5\% , p < 3 × 10 − 5 p<3{\times}10^{-5} ; 10-seed paired validation) while providing no benefit for electronic or steric tasks.
Three lines of evidence confirm this selectivity has a physical rather than statistical basis: improvement is larger under scaffold splits than random splits ( + 11.9 % +11.9\% vs. + 8.5 % +8.5\% on ESOL), concentrates on large, flexible molecules ( + 18.9 % +18.9\% for heaviest quartile), and grows monotonically with training data.
We establish a four-tier performance hierarchy: end-to-end 3D GNNs (SchNet, PaiNN; 21–42% over fingerprints) ≈ \approx engineered physicochemical descriptors (PMI/SASA/USR) > > Morgan fingerprints + XGBoost > > all neural conformer ensemble methods, confirmed by two architecturally diverse GNNs and revealing that the pre-computed feature bottleneck limits ensemble approaches.
Feature attribution and mutual information analysis expose the mechanistic asymmetry: conformer mean features carry 2–8 × \times more information per feature than fingerprint bits, yet covariance features contribute < < 2% of model signal, explaining why five simple scalar invariants outperform all complex covariance architectures ( p < 0.001 p<0.001 ).
These findings yield an empirical property taxonomy and a practical decision framework for when conformer generation is worth the investment.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text: Molecular property prediction is a cornerstone of computational chemistry and drug discovery. While graph neural networks (GNNs) operating on 2D molecular graphs have achieved remarkable success ( Gilmer et al., 2017 ; Yang et al., 2019 ) , a molecule’s biological activity fundamentally depends on its three-dimensional geometry. Small molecules adopt multiple low-energy conformations in solution, and properties such as solvation free energy and lipophilicity are Boltzmann-weighted averages over this conformational ensemble ( Hawkins, 2017 ) . Accurate prediction of solvation properties is particularly critical for ADMET (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity) profiling in early-stage drug discovery ( Lipinski et al., 2001 ; Huuskonen, 2000 ) , where experimental measurement is expensive and computational screening must efficiently prioritize candidates (Figure 1 ). Figure 1 . Mechanistic context for molecular property prediction. Oral drugs must dissolve (aqueous solubility), cross epithelial membranes (lipophilicity), and reach their cellular target. The DKO pipeline predicts these solvation-dependent properties from conformer ensemble statistics. Created with BioRender.com ( BioRender, 2025 ) . Schematic showing three stages of oral drug delivery: pill dissolving in stomach (aqueous solubility), molecule crossing intestinal epithelium into bloodstream (membrane permeability via lipophilicity), and molecule binding to cell surface receptor (target binding). Labels indicate molecular properties predicted by the DKO pipeline. This has motivated a growing body of work on conformer ensemble methods ( Zhu et al., 2024 ; Ganea et al., 2021 ; Stark et al., 2022 ) and 3D-aware GNNs ( Schütt et al., 2017 ; Gasteiger et al., 2020b ; Schütt et al., 2021 ) , which incorporate 3D geometry for property prediction. However, a fundamental question remains unanswered: when does explicit 3D conformer geometry provide signal beyond what 2D molecular descriptors already capture, and why? Prior work has shown that classical descriptors often match neural methods ( Wu et al., 2018 ) and that conformer ensembles help on steric tasks ( Zhu et al., 2024 ) , but no study has systematically characterized which property types benefit from 3D conformer information, with mechanistic explanation and rigorous statistical validation. We address this gap through 13 model configurations across 14 regression targets spanning three benchmark families (MoleculeNet, QM9, MARCEL). Using Distribution Kernel Operators (DKOs), we extract first-order (mean 𝝁 \boldsymbol{\mu} ) and second-order (covariance 𝚺 \boldsymbol{\Sigma} ) statistics from conformer ensembles and evaluate multiple fusion architectures, alongside end-to-end 3D GNN baselines (SchNet, PaiNN). We investigate three concrete research questions: RQ1. Property taxonomy : We characterize which molecular property types benefit from 3D conformer geometry and provide a mechanistic basis for the observed selectivity. RQ2. Representation hierarchy : We establish how pre-computed conformer ensemble methods compare to 2D fingerprints and end-to-end 3D GNNs (SchNet, PaiNN) across task types. RQ3. Representation complexity : We test whether complex covariance representations outperform simple summary statistics, grounded in a bias-variance analysis of parameterization complexity versus dataset size. Scope: This study evaluates hybrid FP+conformer methods on both regression (14 targets) and classification (BACE, BBBP) tasks; end-to-end neural DKO variants are evaluated on regression only, as classification requires architectural adaptation (Section 4.8 ). Our key contributions are: (1) Empirical property taxonomy (Figure 4 ): An evidence-based framework for when conformer geometry adds value, grounded in feature attribution, mutual information analysis, and error stratification. Solvation-dependent properties benefit from hybrid features; steric/Boltzmann properties benefit from attention-based conformer weighting; electronic properties show no improvement. This provides practitioners a decision framework for when to invest in conformer generation. (2) Selective complementarity with mechanistic explanation : Hybrid FP+conformer features yield statistically significant improvements on solvation tasks (ESOL − 11.0 % -11.0\% , p < 10 − 9 p<10^{-9} ; FreeSolv − 13.5 % -13.5\% , p < 3 × 10 − 5 p<3\times 10^{-5} ; 10-seed paired t t -tests). Critically, ESOL improvement is larger under scaffold splits ( + 11.9 % +11.9\% ) than random splits ( + 8.5 % +8.5\% ), ruling out data leakage. The benefit concentrates on large, flexible molecules, consistent with the physical mechanism. (3) Performance hierarchy : End-to-end 3D GNNs (SchNet, PaiNN) surpass fingerprints by 21–42% on solvation tasks, while fingerprints outperform all neural conformer ensemble methods across every benchmark. Enhanced physicochemical 3D descriptors (PMI, SASA, USR) achieve comparable gains to SchNet on ESOL. Two architecturally diverse GNNs (continuous-filter and equivariant) confirm this hierarchy—not previously established—revealing that the pre-computed feature bottleneck, not the absence of 3D information, limits conformer ensemble methods. (4) DKO framework : A Distribution Kernel Operator architecture with 7 covariance representation variants, 28 enhanced 3D descriptors, and a gated fusion mechanism that significantly outperforms attention ( p < 0.001 p<0.001 ). Five simple covariance summary statistics outperform all complex representations.

sections.heading: 2. Related Work
sections.text: The MARCEL benchmark ( Zhu et al., 2024 ) established standardized evaluation for conformer ensemble learning on Kraken steric descriptors, bond dissociation energies, and electronic properties. GeoMol ( Ganea et al., 2021 ) generates conformers via end-to-end learning, while 3D Infomax ( Stark et al., 2022 ) uses contrastive 3D pre-training to enrich 2D representations. Alternative conformer generation methods include OMEGA ( Hawkins et al., 2010 ) and CREST ( Pracht et al., 2020 ) ; we use ETKDG for consistency with the MARCEL protocol. These approaches typically aggregate conformer features via mean pooling or attention, discarding distributional information. In the 3D representation space, SchNet ( Schütt et al., 2017 ) introduced continuous-filter convolutions for 3D coordinates; DimeNet++ ( Gasteiger et al., 2020a ) adds directional message passing; PaiNN ( Schütt et al., 2021 ) achieves equivariant message passing; and Equiformer ( Liao and Smidt, 2023 ) combines equivariant attention with transformers. These methods operate on single conformers; our work instead models the ensemble distribution via summary statistics. On the pre-training front, GROVER ( Rong et al., 2020 ) uses self-supervised graph transformers on large molecular corpora. These pre-trained models ( Zhou et al., 2023 ; Rong et al., 2020 ) often achieve state-of-the-art results on MoleculeNet benchmarks but require large-scale pre-training data. We do not benchmark pre-trained models, as our focus is understanding when 3D conformer geometry per se adds predictive value—an orthogonal question to whether pre-training on large molecular corpora helps. This scoping decision means our property taxonomy is validated in the non-pre-trained setting; pre-trained 3D models such as Uni-Mol ( Zhou et al., 2023 ) may extract useful 3D signals even for electronic properties through learned representations trained on millions of conformers, which could alter the taxonomy boundaries. We explicitly note this as a limitation (Section 6 ). Importantly, DKO conformer statistics are complementary to pre-trained representations: conformer 𝝁 \boldsymbol{\mu} / 𝚺 \boldsymbol{\Sigma} features could be concatenated with pre-trained embeddings just as they are concatenated with fingerprints here, potentially compounding improvements on solvation tasks. We leave this combination for future work. Among classical approaches, extended-connectivity fingerprints ( Rogers and Hahn, 2010 ) remain the dominant representation in cheminformatics. Combined with gradient-boosted trees ( Chen and Guestrin, 2016 ) , they provide baselines that neural methods frequently fail to surpass ( Wu et al., 2018 ; Jiang et al., 2021 ) . Jiang et al. ( Jiang et al., 2021 ) systematically showed that descriptor-based models outperform GNNs on many drug discovery tasks, a finding our work extends to the 3D conformer domain. Our work quantifies this gap and identifies where conformer features add complementary value. Processing unordered conformer sets also requires permutation-invariant architectures. DeepSets ( Zaheer et al., 2017 ) provides the theoretical foundation, while Set Transformer ( Lee et al., 2019 ) introduces attention-based aggregation. We compare these against our DKO framework, which models the distribution’s first and second moments explicitly. More broadly, kernel methods have a long history in molecular property prediction ( Rupp et al., 2012 ) . Our DKO builds on distributional kernels that compare molecules via their conformer distributions, using a learned positive semi-definite kernel 𝐊 = 𝐋𝐋 ⊤ \mathbf{K}=\mathbf{L}\mathbf{L}^{\top} .

sections.heading: 3.1. Conformer Generation and Feature Extraction
sections.text: For each molecule, we generate n = 50 n=50 conformers using RDKit’s ( Landrum, 2016 ) ETKDG (Experimental Torsion-angle preference with Knowledge and Distance Geometry) algorithm ( Riniker and Landrum, 2015 ) with energy minimization via the MMFF94 (Merck Molecular Force Field) force field. The choice of n = 50 n{=}50 follows the MARCEL benchmark protocol ( Zhu et al., 2024 ) ; conformer count ablations (Appendix E ) show that n = 5 n{=}5 – 10 10 suffice for XGBoost-based models. Unlike MARCEL, which uses Boltzmann-weighted conformer aggregation, our pipeline computes unweighted mean and covariance statistics. This simplification reduces implementation complexity but may underweight low-energy conformers that dominate the thermodynamic ensemble, particularly for Boltzmann-averaged properties (Section 4.7 ). From each conformer’s 3D coordinates, we compute a feature vector 𝐱 i ∈ ℝ D \mathbf{x}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} via the following procedure: for each pair of atoms within a 4.0 4.0 Å cutoff, we compute the interatomic distance; for each bonded triple, the bond angle; and for each bonded quadruple, the torsion angle (encoded as cos ⁡ θ , sin ⁡ θ \cos\theta,\sin\theta ). These geometric features are concatenated with 19-dimensional per-atom features (element type, hybridization, formal charge, etc.) and zero-padded or truncated to dimension D D . DKO neural models use D = 1024 D=1024 . For the XGBoost hybrid, 𝝁 \boldsymbol{\mu} is computed from features truncated to D = 256 D=256 ; a sensitivity analysis sweeping D ∈ { 256,512 , 1024 , 2048 } D\in\{256,512,1024,2048\} (Section 4.9 ) confirms D = 256 D=256 is optimal: larger D D adds noise dimensions that the shallow model cannot exploit, and RMSE monotonically increases with D D . Given a conformer ensemble { 𝐱 1 , … , 𝐱 n } \{\mathbf{x}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{n}\} , we compute: (1) 𝝁 \displaystyle\boldsymbol{\mu} = 1 n ​ ∑ i = 1 n 𝐱 i ∈ ℝ D , \displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{x}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{D}, (2) 𝚺 \displaystyle\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = 1 n − 1 ​ ∑ i = 1 n ( 𝐱 i − 𝝁 ) ​ ( 𝐱 i − 𝝁 ) ⊤ + λ ​ 𝐈 ∈ ℝ D × D , \displaystyle=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\mathbf{x}_{i}-\boldsymbol{\mu})(\mathbf{x}_{i}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^{\top}+\lambda\mathbf{I}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times D}, where λ = 10 − 2 \lambda=10^{-2} provides regularization against near-singular covariance matrices.

sections.heading: 3.4. Enhanced 3D Shape Descriptors
sections.text: We implement 28 property-relevant 3D descriptors in four categories: shape (9: 2 PMI ratios, 3 raw principal moments, asphericity, eccentricity, radius of gyration, inertial shape factor), surface (1: total SASA ( Mitternacht, 2016 ) ), USR (12: rotation-invariant shape signature ( Ballester and Richards, 2007 ) ), and global geometry (6: span, molecular volume, compactness, 3 bounding box extents). These capture physically relevant 3D variation—SASA relates to solvation free energy, PMI ratios encode shape anisotropy.

sections.heading: 3.5. Hybrid FP + Conformer Approach
sections.text: To test complementarity, we concatenate Morgan fingerprints (2048-bit, radius 2) with conformer statistics: (3) 𝐳 = [ FP 2048 ; 𝝁 d ; 𝝈 5 ] ∈ ℝ 2048 + d + 5 , \mathbf{z}=[\text{FP}_{2048};\;\boldsymbol{\mu}_{d};\;\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{5}]\in\mathbb{R}^{2048+d+5}, where 𝝁 d \boldsymbol{\mu}_{d} is the conformer mean projected to d = 256 d{=}256 dimensions via PCA, and 𝝈 5 \boldsymbol{\sigma}_{5} denotes 5 variance-based summary statistics from 𝚺 \boldsymbol{\Sigma} (total variance, top-5 eigenvalue variance, maximum eigenvalue, effective rank, mean eigenvalue variance). We train XGBoost ( Chen and Guestrin, 2016 ) on these combined features (comparison with a neural MLP in Appendix G ).

sections.text: We quantify conformer diversity per molecule as CDM = tr ​ ( 𝚺 ) = ∑ i = 1 D λ i \text{CDM}=\text{tr}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})=\sum_{i=1}^{D}\lambda_{i} , the total variance across all conformer features. High CDM indicates large geometric variation; per-dataset statistics are in Appendix C .

sections.heading: 3.7. Training Details
sections.text: All DKO and baseline neural models are trained with AdamW ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019 ) (learning rate 10 − 4 10^{-4} , weight decay 10 − 5 10^{-5} ), 300 epochs with early stopping (patience 30), and feature normalization along the conformer dimension only ( dim = 1 \text{dim}=1 ). Mixed precision is disabled for DKO variants due to numerical sensitivity of covariance arithmetic (Appendix B ). We use 3 seeds for the main benchmark and 10 seeds for statistical validation; 10 seeds provide sufficient power to detect effect sizes of ∼ 5 % {\sim}5\% at α = 0.05 \alpha=0.05 given the observed variance across architectures. All datasets use Murcko scaffold-based 80/10/10 train/validation/test splits ( Bemis and Murcko, 1996 ) , where molecules sharing the same core scaffold are kept in the same split. Scaffold splits are generated by extracting the Bemis–Murcko generic scaffold ( Bemis and Murcko, 1996 ) for each molecule using RDKit, sorting scaffolds by frequency, and assigning entire scaffold groups to train/validation/test in order until the 80/10/10 ratio is met. For the main benchmark, each model configuration is evaluated over 3 independent seeds (controlling weight initialization and data shuffling); for statistical validation experiments (Section 4.10 ), we use 10 seeds to provide sufficient power to detect effect sizes of ∼ 5 % {\sim}5\% at α = 0.05 \alpha=0.05 . We additionally compare scaffold vs. random splits to quantify generalization to unseen chemical scaffolds (Section 4.11 ).

sections.heading: 4.1. Datasets
sections.text: We evaluate on three dataset categories: MoleculeNet regression ( Wu et al., 2018 ) : ESOL (1,128 molecules, aqueous solubility ( Delaney, 2004 ) ), FreeSolv (642, hydration free energy ( Mobley and Guthrie, 2014 ) ), Lipophilicity (4,200, octanol–water partition coefficient), and QM9 (133,885 molecules ( Ramakrishnan et al., 2014 ) ; we predict three targets: HOMO–LUMO gap, HOMO energy, and LUMO energy, denoted QM9-Gap, QM9-HOMO, QM9-LUMO). MARCEL benchmark ( Zhu et al., 2024 ) : Kraken ( Gensch et al., 2022 ) (1,552 phosphine ligands, 4 Sterimol steric descriptors (B5, L, buried-B5, buried-L)—Boltzmann-averaged 3D properties), BDE (5,915 bond dissociation energies), Drugs-75K (75,099 drug-like molecules, 3 electronic properties). sections.text: To establish an upper bound for end-to-end 3D learning, we train two architecturally diverse 3D GNNs: SchNet ( Schütt et al., 2017 ) (continuous-filter convolutions, equivariant under translations/rotations) and PaiNN ( Schütt et al., 2021 ) (equivariant message passing with separate scalar/vector channels). The convergence of gains (21–42%) across two fundamentally different architectures confirms that the hierarchy is robust to model choice. On ESOL, FP+3D descriptors match SchNet (1.000 vs. 1.004), suggesting engineered physicochemical features can approach end-to-end 3D learning at a fraction of the computational cost. We selected SchNet and PaiNN as 3D GNN baselines because they represent the two principal paradigms in geometric deep learning for molecules: SchNet uses continuous-filter convolutions that are invariant to rotation and translation, while PaiNN employs equivariant message passing with separate scalar and vector channels. The convergence of 21–42% gains across two architecturally diverse GNNs with fundamentally different inductive biases (continuous-filter vs. equivariant) provides strong evidence that the observed hierarchy reflects a genuine property of the representation, not an artifact of a single architecture.

sections.heading: 4.13. Error Analysis by Molecular Properties
sections.text: Error stratification by molecular properties (Appendices L , O ) reveals that ESOL hybrid improvement concentrates on large, flexible molecules: + 18.9 % +18.9\% for heaviest quartile, + 39.7 % +39.7\% for molecules with 1–2 rotatable bonds, while rigid molecules show no benefit ( − 0.3 % -0.3\% ). This is consistent with the physical mechanism: conformer ensembles carry meaningful signal only when the molecule samples diverse conformations.

sections.heading: 4.14. Why Fingerprints Dominate: A Mechanistic Analysis
sections.text: Feature attribution (Appendix I ) and mutual information analysis (Appendix H ) explain the heterogeneous improvement pattern. Conformer 𝝁 \boldsymbol{\mu} features carry 2–8 × \times more MI per feature than fingerprint bits, yet the hybrid benefit depends on dataset-specific complementarity: ESOL improvement is 𝝁 \boldsymbol{\mu} -driven (67.4% attribution), FreeSolv is FP-driven with 𝝁 \boldsymbol{\mu} complementing (62/37%), and QM9-Gap shows no improvement because FP and 𝝁 \boldsymbol{\mu} are already balanced (49/49%). Covariance ( 𝚺 \boldsymbol{\Sigma} ) features contribute < < 2% of importance everywhere, and conditional MI of 𝚺 \boldsymbol{\Sigma} given 𝝁 \boldsymbol{\mu} is slightly negative (Table 19 ), suggesting covariance features are largely redundant in information-theoretic terms once mean features are available, though they still provide a statistically significant marginal RMSE improvement on solvation tasks (Table 10 ).

sections.heading: 4.15. Ablation: Why Simple Covariance Representations Win
sections.text: The top-10 eigenvalues of 𝚺 \boldsymbol{\Sigma} capture only 4–8% of total variance, with effective rank at 90% explained variance ranging from 353 to 685. This explains why complex representations (lowrank, eigenspectrum) overfit while 5 scalar invariants succeed: they extract information-dense statistics without the overfitting risk of high-dimensional parameterizations on datasets of 642–4,200 molecules. Synthetic validation and eigenvalue analysis details are in Appendix Q .

Our results reveal a consistent empirical pattern across molecular properties with respect to conformer geometry, which we formalize as a property taxonomy for conformer utility (Figure 4 ). Solvation properties (ESOL, FreeSolv) show statistically significant hybrid improvement (11–14%, p < 10 − 4 p<10^{-4} ; Tables 10 , 11 , 25 ), robust to scaffold splitting, growing with training data, and concentrated on large, flexible molecules—consistent with the physical mechanism that conformer diversity carries signal only when molecules sample diverse conformations. For steric/Boltzmann properties (Kraken), attention wins on buried descriptors while mean aggregation wins on standard ones; DKO performs worst, suggesting covariance statistics lose per-conformer detail important for Boltzmann-averaged properties. Electronic properties (QM9-Gap, QM9-LUMO, BDE, Drugs-75K) show no hybrid improvement; fingerprints alone suffice, consistent with these properties being determined by equilibrium electronic structure rather than conformational variation. These three property categories are cross-cut by a representation hierarchy . Two architecturally diverse 3D GNNs (SchNet, PaiNN) exceed FP+XGBoost by 21–42% on solvation tasks, confirming that the pre-computed feature bottleneck—not the lack of 3D information—limits hybrid approaches. The hierarchy is: (1) end-to-end 3D GNNs, which learn task-specific geometric representations from atomic coordinates; (2) engineered 3D descriptors (FP + PMI/SASA/USR), matching GNN performance on ESOL (1.000 vs. 1.004); (3) 2D fingerprints + XGBoost; and (4) neural conformer ensemble methods. Moving from tier 4 to tier 1 corresponds to progressively richer preservation of 3D relational structure: DKO discards it into summary statistics, engineered descriptors preserve selected physical invariants, and GNNs retain the full atomic graph. A striking finding is that simpler covariance representations consistently outperform complex ones. The full 𝚺 ∈ ℝ D × D \boldsymbol{\Sigma}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times D} contains D ⁡ ( D + 1 ) / 2 ≈ 524,288 D(D+1)/2\approx 524{,}288 unique entries ( D = 1024 D{=}1024 ), exceeding training set sizes by 125–815 × \times —the regime where the Ledoit-Wolf estimator ( Ledoit and Wolf, 2004 ) collapses toward the identity. Our 5 scalar invariants extract sufficient statistics without high-dimensional parameterization. From a model selection perspective, the invariants operate at ∼ 180 {\sim}180 samples per parameter on ESOL ( N train ≈ 900 N_{\text{train}}\approx 900 ), while the lowrank variant ( k = 128 k{=}128 ) operates at ∼ 7 {\sim}7 —well below reliable estimation thresholds. The feature dimension ablation (Table 9 ) confirms independently that RMSE monotonically degrades from D = 256 D{=}256 to D = 2,048 D{=}2{,}048 even for 𝝁 \boldsymbol{\mu} , demonstrating that the bias-variance tradeoff penalizes higher-dimensional representations at these sample sizes. The “pre-computed feature bottleneck” thus reflects a fundamental statistical constraint: summary statistics are effective because they compress O ⁡ ( D 2 ) O(D^{2}) distributional information into O ⁡ ( 1 ) O(1) reliably estimable parameters. The taxonomy covers 3 solvation, 4 steric, and 7 electronic regression targets plus 2 classification targets; properties with mixed character (e.g., membrane permeability) may not fit neatly, and the taxonomy should be conditioned on data availability (FreeSolv improvement emerges only above ∼ {\sim} 440 molecules). Our findings extend several lines of prior work. MARCEL ( Zhu et al., 2024 ) showed conformer methods help on Kraken steric descriptors but did not evaluate hybrid approaches or solvation tasks; we extend Wu et al. ( Wu et al., 2018 ) and Jiang et al. ( Jiang et al., 2021 ) by identifying which property types benefit from 3D information with mechanistic grounding. Our goal is understanding when conformer geometry helps, not SOTA performance (published SOTA uses different splits and protocols ( Heid et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2023 ) ). Large pre-trained models ( Zhou et al., 2023 ; Rong et al., 2020 ) address an orthogonal question; DKO conformer statistics could augment pre-trained embeddings to compound improvements on solvation tasks. From a practical standpoint, our results suggest: (1) always start with Morgan FP + XGBoost as a baseline, (2) if the property involves solvation or flexibility and the dataset contains > > 500 molecules, add conformer 𝝁 \boldsymbol{\mu} and 𝚺 \boldsymbol{\Sigma} invariants—expect the largest gains for large, flexible molecules with multiple rotatable bonds, (3) consider enhanced physicochemical 3D descriptors (PMI, SASA, USR) which can outperform raw geometric features, and (4) for maximum accuracy, end-to-end 3D GNNs (SchNet, PaiNN) provide the strongest results. The scaffold split validation ensures these recommendations generalize to novel chemical scaffolds, not just structurally similar compounds.

sections.heading: 6. Conclusion
sections.text: We presented a systematic study of when 3D conformer geometry complements 2D molecular fingerprints across 14 regression and 2 classification targets. Our main findings are: (1) an empirical property taxonomy—conformer statistics selectively help solvation-dependent properties ( p < 10 − 4 p<10^{-4} , scaffold-split validated) but not electronic or steric tasks; (2) a four-tier performance hierarchy confirmed by two architecturally diverse GNNs, revealing that the pre-computed feature bottleneck limits conformer ensemble methods; (3) mechanistic understanding grounded in feature attribution and mutual information; and (4) a bias-variance analysis explaining why 5 scalar invariants outperform complex covariance representations. For practitioners: start with Morgan FP + XGBoost; add conformer 𝝁 \boldsymbol{\mu} for solvation properties with > > 500 molecules; consider PMI/SASA/USR descriptors; use 3D GNNs when accuracy justifies cost. Five to ten conformers suffice. Several limitations should be noted. Our conformer features use RDKit ETKDG with uniform (not Boltzmann) weights. Auxiliary experiments re-split data independently, so FP-only baselines vary slightly across tables (up to ∼ 6 % {\sim}6\% ). The hybrid uses simple concatenation; learned feature interaction might yield larger gains. Our evaluation spans academic benchmarks (642–133K molecules); validation on larger industrial datasets (ChEMBL, ZINC) would strengthen generalizability. The taxonomy is validated in the non-pre-trained setting; pre-trained 3D models (Uni-Mol, GROVER) may shift its boundaries. Future work should combine DKO statistics with pre-trained representations and validate at larger scale. sections.heading: Appendix B Implementation Sensitivity Analysis
sections.text: The DKO implementation is sensitive to several hyperparameters, identified through systematic ablation: (1) Learning rate ( 10 − 5 10^{-5} vs 10 − 4 10^{-4} ): Using a 10 × 10\times lower learning rate than other models reduced ESOL RMSE by 30 % 30\% ( 3.318 → 2.309 3.318\to 2.309 ) when corrected. (2) Feature normalization ( dim = ( 1 , 2 ) \text{dim}{=}(1,2) vs dim = 1 \text{dim}{=}1 ): Normalizing across both conformers and features destroyed inter-feature variance in 𝚺 \boldsymbol{\Sigma} , making all covariance features approximately identical. Correcting to dim = 1 \text{dim}{=}1 restored Pearson correlation from ∼ 0 {\sim}0 to ∼ 0.48 {\sim}0.48 . (3) Kernel output dimension ( 32 32 vs 64 64 ): Marginal individual effect but needed for combined benefit. (4) Sigma regularization ( 10 − 4 10^{-4} vs 10 − 2 10^{-2} ): Too-small regularization caused near-singular covariance matrices. (5) Mixed precision : FP16 arithmetic is insufficient for covariance matrix operations. Enabling mixed precision increased RMSE by 30 % 30\% with 10 × 10\times higher variance. Combined, these corrections improved DKO’s ESOL R 2 R^{2} from − 1.70 -1.70 to − 0.04 -0.04 , a swing of 1.66 1.66 in explained variance. The sensitivity of covariance-based methods to numerical precision and normalization choices is an important practical consideration.

When do three-dimensional conformer ensembles improve molecular property prediction beyond two-dimensional fingerprints? We provide the first systematic, mechanistically grounded answer. Through ∼ {\sim} 1,000 experiments spanning 13 model configurations, 14 regression targets, and 2 classification targets across MoleculeNet, QM9, and MARCEL benchmarks, we discover selective complementarity : conformer ensemble statistics extracted via Distribution Kernel Operators (DKOs) yield statistically significant RMSE reductions on solvation-dependent properties (ESOL − 11.0 % -11.0\% , p < 10 − 9 p<10^{-9} ; FreeSolv − 13.5 % -13.5\% , p < 3 × 10 − 5 p<3{\times}10^{-5} ; 10-seed paired validation) while providing no benefit for electronic or steric tasks. Three lines of evidence confirm this selectivity has a physical rather than statistical basis: improvement is larger under scaffold splits than random splits ( + 11.9 % +11.9\% vs. + 8.5 % +8.5\% on ESOL), concentrates on large, flexible molecules ( + 18.9 % +18.9\% for heaviest quartile), and grows monotonically with training data. We establish a four-tier performance hierarchy: end-to-end 3D GNNs (SchNet, PaiNN; 21–42% over fingerprints) ≈ \approx engineered physicochemical descriptors (PMI/SASA/USR) > > Morgan fingerprints + XGBoost > > all neural conformer ensemble methods, confirmed by two architecturally diverse GNNs and revealing that the pre-computed feature bottleneck limits ensemble approaches. Feature attribution and mutual information analysis expose the mechanistic asymmetry: conformer mean features carry 2–8 × \times more information per feature than fingerprint bits, yet covariance features contribute < < 2% of model signal, explaining why five simple scalar invariants outperform all complex covariance architectures ( p < 0.001 p<0.001 ). These findings yield an empirical property taxonomy and a practical decision framework for when conformer generation is worth the investment. Keywords: molecular property prediction, conformer ensembles, distribution kernel operators, fingerprints, 3D descriptors, covariance representations 1. Introduction Molecular property prediction is a cornerstone of computational chemistry and drug discovery. While graph neural networks (GNNs) operating on 2D molecular graphs have achieved remarkable success ( Gilmer et al., 2017 ; Yang et al., 2019 ) , a molecule’s biological activity fundamentally depends on its three-dimensional geometry. Small molecules adopt multiple low-energy conformations in solution, and properties such as solvation free energy and lipophilicity are Boltzmann-weighted averages over this conformational ensemble ( Hawkins, 2017 ) . Accurate prediction of solvation properties is particularly critical for ADMET (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity) profiling in early-stage drug discovery ( Lipinski et al., 2001 ; Huuskonen, 2000 ) , where experimental measurement is expensive and computational screening must efficiently prioritize candidates (Figure 1 ). Figure 1 . Mechanistic context for molecular property prediction. Oral drugs must dissolve (aqueous solubility), cross epithelial membranes (lipophilicity), and reach their cellular target. The DKO pipeline predicts these solvation-dependent properties from conformer ensemble statistics. Created with BioRender.com ( BioRender, 2025 ) . Schematic showing three stages of oral drug delivery: pill dissolving in stomach (aqueous solubility), molecule crossing intestinal epithelium into bloodstream (membrane permeability via lipophilicity), and molecule binding to cell surface receptor (target binding). Labels indicate molecular properties predicted by the DKO pipeline. This has motivated a growing body of work on conformer ensemble methods ( Zhu et al., 2024 ; Ganea et al., 2021 ; Stark et al., 2022 ) and 3D-aware GNNs ( Schütt et al., 2017 ; Gasteiger et al., 2020b ; Schütt et al., 2021 ) , which incorporate 3D geometry for property prediction. However, a fundamental question remains unanswered: when does explicit 3D conformer geometry provide signal beyond what 2D molecular descriptors already capture, and why? Prior work has shown that classical descriptors often match neural methods ( Wu et al., 2018 ) and that conformer ensembles help on steric tasks ( Zhu et al., 2024 ) , but no study has systematically characterized which property types benefit from 3D conformer information, with mechanistic explanation and rigorous statistical validation. We address this gap through 13 model configurations across 14 regression targets spanning three benchmark families (MoleculeNet, QM9, MARCEL). Using Distribution Kernel Operators (DKOs), we extract first-order (mean 𝝁 \boldsymbol{\mu} ) and second-order (covariance 𝚺 \boldsymbol{\Sigma} ) statistics from conformer ensembles and evaluate multiple fusion architectures, alongside end-to-end 3D GNN baselines (SchNet, PaiNN). We investigate three concrete research questions: RQ1. Property taxonomy : We characterize which molecular property types benefit from 3D conformer geometry and provide a mechanistic basis for the observed selectivity. RQ2. Representation hierarchy : We establish how pre-computed conformer ensemble methods compare to 2D fingerprints and end-to-end 3D GNNs (SchNet, PaiNN) across task types. RQ3. Representation complexity : We test whether complex covariance representations outperform simple summary statistics, grounded in a bias-variance analysis of parameterization complexity versus dataset size. Scope: This study evaluates hybrid FP+conformer methods on both regression (14 targets) and classification (BACE, BBBP) tasks; end-to-end neural DKO variants are evaluated on regression only, as classification requires architectural adaptation (Section 4.8 ). Our key contributions are: (1) Empirical property taxonomy (Figure 4 ): An evidence-based framework for when conformer geometry adds value, grounded in feature attribution, mutual information analysis, and error stratification. Solvation-dependent properties benefit from hybrid features; steric/Boltzmann properties benefit from attention-based conformer weighting; electronic properties show no improvement. This provides practitioners a decision framework for when to invest in conformer generation. (2) Selective complementarity with mechanistic explanation : Hybrid FP+conformer features yield statistically significant improvements on solvation tasks (ESOL − 11.0 % -11.0\% , p < 10 − 9 p<10^{-9} ; FreeSolv − 13.5 % -13.5\% , p < 3 × 10 − 5 p<3\times 10^{-5} ; 10-seed paired t t -tests). Critically, ESOL improvement is larger under scaffold splits ( + 11.9 % +11.9\% ) than random splits ( + 8.5 % +8.5\% ), ruling out data leakage. The benefit concentrates on large, flexible molecules, consistent with the physical mechanism. (3) Performance hierarchy : End-to-end 3D GNNs (SchNet, PaiNN) surpass fingerprints by 21–42% on solvation tasks, while fingerprints outperform all neural conformer ensemble methods across every benchmark. Enhanced physicochemical 3D descriptors (PMI, SASA, USR) achieve comparable gains to SchNet on ESOL. Two architecturally diverse GNNs (continuous-filter and equivariant) confirm this hierarchy—not previously established—revealing that the pre-computed feature bottleneck, not the absence of 3D information, limits conformer ensemble methods. (4) DKO framework : A Distribution Kernel Operator architecture with 7 covariance representation variants, 28 enhanced 3D descriptors, and a gated fusion mechanism that significantly outperforms attention ( p < 0.001 p<0.001 ). Five simple covariance summary statistics outperform all complex representations. 2. Related Work The MARCEL benchmark ( Zhu et al., 2024 ) established standardized evaluation for conformer ensemble learning on Kraken steric descriptors, bond dissociation energies, and electronic properties. GeoMol ( Ganea et al., 2021 ) generates conformers via end-to-end learning, while 3D Infomax ( Stark et al., 2022 ) uses contrastive 3D pre-training to enrich 2D representations. Alternative conformer generation methods include OMEGA ( Hawkins et al., 2010 ) and CREST ( Pracht et al., 2020 ) ; we use ETKDG for consistency with the MARCEL protocol. These approaches typically aggregate conformer features via mean pooling or attention, discarding distributional information. In the 3D representation space, SchNet ( Schütt et al., 2017 ) introduced continuous-filter convolutions for 3D coordinates; DimeNet++ ( Gasteiger et al., 2020a ) adds directional message passing; PaiNN ( Schütt et al., 2021 ) achieves equivariant message passing; and Equiformer ( Liao and Smidt, 2023 ) combines equivariant attention with transformers. These methods operate on single conformers; our work instead models the ensemble distribution via summary statistics. On the pre-training front, GROVER ( Rong et al., 2020 ) uses self-supervised graph transformers on large molecular corpora. These pre-trained models ( Zhou et al., 2023 ; Rong et al., 2020 ) often achieve state-of-the-art results on MoleculeNet benchmarks but require large-scale pre-training data. We do not benchmark pre-trained models, as our focus is understanding when 3D conformer geometry per se adds predictive value—an orthogonal question to whether pre-training on large molecular corpora helps. This scoping decision means our property taxonomy is validated in the non-pre-trained setting; pre-trained 3D models such as Uni-Mol ( Zhou et al., 2023 ) may extract useful 3D signals even for electronic properties through learned representations trained on millions of conformers, which could alter the taxonomy boundaries. We explicitly note this as a limitation (Section 6 ). Importantly, DKO conformer statistics are complementary to pre-trained representations: conformer 𝝁 \boldsymbol{\mu} / 𝚺 \boldsymbol{\Sigma} features could be concatenated with pre-trained embeddings just as they are concatenated with fingerprints here, potentially compounding improvements on solvation tasks. We leave this combination for future work. Among classical approaches, extended-connectivity fingerprints ( Rogers and Hahn, 2010 ) remain the dominant representation in cheminformatics. Combined with gradient-boosted trees ( Chen and Guestrin, 2016 ) , they provide baselines that neural methods frequently fail to surpass ( Wu et al., 2018 ; Jiang et al., 2021 ) . Jiang et al. ( Jiang et al., 2021 ) systematically showed that descriptor-based models outperform GNNs on many drug discovery tasks, a finding our work extends to the 3D conformer domain. Our work quantifies this gap and identifies where conformer features add complementary value. Processing unordered conformer sets also requires permutation-invariant architectures. DeepSets ( Zaheer et al., 2017 ) provides the theoretical foundation, while Set Transformer ( Lee et al., 2019 ) introduces attention-based aggregation. We compare these against our DKO framework, which models the distribution’s first and second moments explicitly. More broadly, kernel methods have a long history in molecular property prediction ( Rupp et al., 2012 ) . Our DKO builds on distributional kernels that compare molecules via their conformer distributions, using a learned positive semi-definite kernel 𝐊 = 𝐋𝐋 ⊤ \mathbf{K}=\mathbf{L}\mathbf{L}^{\top} . 3. Figure 2 provides an overview of the DKO pipeline and hybrid approach. 3.1. Conformer Generation and Feature Extraction For each molecule, we generate n = 50 n=50 conformers using RDKit’s ( Landrum, 2016 ) ETKDG (Experimental Torsion-angle preference with Knowledge and Distance Geometry) algorithm ( Riniker and Landrum, 2015 ) with energy minimization via the MMFF94 (Merck Molecular Force Field) force field. The choice of n = 50 n{=}50 follows the MARCEL benchmark protocol ( Zhu et al., 2024 ) ; conformer count ablations (Appendix E ) show that n = 5 n{=}5 – 10 10 suffice for XGBoost-based models. Unlike MARCEL, which uses Boltzmann-weighted conformer aggregation, our pipeline computes unweighted mean and covariance statistics. This simplification reduces implementation complexity but may underweight low-energy conformers that dominate the thermodynamic ensemble, particularly for Boltzmann-averaged properties (Section 4.7 ). From each conformer’s 3D coordinates, we compute a feature vector 𝐱 i ∈ ℝ D \mathbf{x}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} via the following procedure: for each pair of atoms within a 4.0 4.0 Å cutoff, we compute the interatomic distance; for each bonded triple, the bond angle; and for each bonded quadruple, the torsion angle (encoded as cos ⁡ θ , sin ⁡ θ \cos\theta,\sin\theta ). These geometric features are concatenated with 19-dimensional per-atom features (element type, hybridization, formal charge, etc.) and zero-padded or truncated to dimension D D . DKO neural models use D = 1024 D=1024 . For the XGBoost hybrid, 𝝁 \boldsymbol{\mu} is computed from features truncated to D = 256 D=256 ; a sensitivity analysis sweeping D ∈ { 256,512 , 1024 , 2048 } D\in\{256,512,1024,2048\} (Section 4.9 ) confirms D = 256 D=256 is optimal: larger D D adds noise dimensions that the shallow model cannot exploit, and RMSE monotonically increases with D D . Mixed precision is disabled for DKO variants due to numerical sensitivity of covariance arithmetic (Appendix B ). We use 3 seeds for the main benchmark and 10 seeds for statistical validation; 10 seeds provide sufficient power to detect effect sizes of ∼ 5 % {\sim}5\% at α = 0.05 \alpha=0.05 given the observed variance across architectures. All datasets use Murcko scaffold-based 80/10/10 train/validation/test splits ( Bemis and Murcko, 1996 ) , where molecules sharing the same core scaffold are kept in the same split. Scaffold splits are generated by extracting the Bemis–Murcko generic scaffold ( Bemis and Murcko, 1996 ) for each molecule using RDKit, sorting scaffolds by frequency, and assigning entire scaffold groups to train/validation/test in order until the 80/10/10 ratio is met. Datasets We evaluate on three dataset categories: MoleculeNet regression ( Wu et al., 2018 ) : ESOL (1,128 molecules, aqueous solubility ( Delaney, 2004 ) ), FreeSolv (642, hydration free energy ( Mobley and Guthrie, 2014 ) ), Lipophilicity (4,200, octanol–water partition coefficient), and QM9 (133,885 molecules ( Ramakrishnan et al., 2014 ) ; we predict three targets: HOMO–LUMO gap, HOMO energy, and LUMO energy, denoted QM9-Gap, QM9-HOMO, QM9-LUMO).
